nameStory: The Glossy Ibis gets its name from the beautiful metallic sheen that glimmers across its dark feathers, especially visible in bright sunlight. The word 'ibis' comes from ancient Egyptian and Greek cultures, where these birds were considered sacred. Interestingly, this species was once called the 'black curlew' in old England, though it's not actually related to curlews at all!
description: The Glossy Ibis is a medium-sized wading bird with a distinctive curved bill that looks like a sickle. At first glance, it appears completely dark or black, but in good light reveals stunning bronze, purple, and green iridescent colors across its feathers. These elegant birds stand about 2 feet tall with long legs perfect for wading through shallow water. They're part of the ibis and spoonbill family, close relatives of herons and egrets.

idTips.label: Curved Sickle Bill
idTips.description: The long, thin bill curves downward like a crescent moon or farming sickle - this curved shape is unmistakable and perfect for probing mud for food

idTips.label: Iridescent Bronze Plumage
idTips.description: What looks black from a distance reveals gorgeous metallic bronze, green, and purple colors up close, like an oil slick shimmering in sunlight

idTips.label: Long Dark Legs
idTips.description: Dark grayish or blackish legs that seem almost too long for the body, perfect for wading through knee-deep marsh water

idTips.label: Neck Position in Flight
idTips.description: Flies with neck extended straight out (unlike herons that fold their necks back), creating a streamlined silhouette

idTips.label: Probing Feeding Behavior
idTips.description: Uses that curved bill like a probe, sweeping and jabbing into soft mud and shallow water with methodical, almost mechanical movements

habitat: Look for Glossy Ibis in freshwater and saltwater marshes, mudflats, shallow ponds, and flooded agricultural fields throughout New England's coastal and inland wetlands. They prefer areas with soft, muddy bottoms where they can easily probe for food, often alongside other wading birds like herons and egrets. You'll most commonly spot them in places like salt marshes along the coast, beaver ponds, and the shallow edges of lakes and rivers.

seasonality.spring: Peak arrival time in New England as birds return from southern wintering grounds. Look for them establishing territories in marshes and beginning courtship displays with their glossy breeding plumage at its most brilliant.
seasonality.summer: Prime viewing season when adults are actively feeding young and most visible as they wade through shallow waters. This is when you're most likely to observe their characteristic probing feeding behavior.
seasonality.fall: Adults and juveniles gather in larger flocks before migration. Young birds appear browner and less glossy than adults, making identification slightly more challenging.
seasonality.winter: Most birds have migrated south, though occasional stragglers may remain in southern New England coastal areas during mild winters.

funFact: Ancient Egyptians considered ibises so sacred that they mummified millions of them - archaeologists have discovered entire underground galleries packed with carefully wrapped ibis mummies, and killing one was punishable by death!
confusionNotes: Often confused with immature night-herons or other dark wading birds at a distance, but that distinctive curved bill is a dead giveaway - no other New England wading bird has such a pronounced downward curve. Remember: if the bill curves like a banana, it's an ibis!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'black curlew' historically, Glossy Ibis are completely unrelated to curlews, which are shorebirds with different feeding habits and habitats. The name confusion arose simply because both species have curved bills, showing how common names can sometimes mislead us about actual relationships between species.
compareHints: While the similar White-faced Ibis occasionally appears in New England, Glossy Ibis lacks the distinctive white border around the face and red eyes that characterize its western cousin. In our region, the Glossy Ibis is much more likely, and during breeding season shows darker eyes and no facial white markings. Both species have the same curved bill and iridescent plumage, but the facial features are the key difference.

relatedSpecies.distinction: White-faced Ibis differs from Glossy Ibis primarily by the white facial border during breeding season and slightly different bill and leg coloration.
